claims.claim: UK GDPR Article 9 lists nine special categories; biometric data counts only when used to identify someone uniquely; age is not among them but is a protected characteristic under section 4 of the Equality Act 2010; special category data needs an Article 6 basis and an Article 9 condition.
Inferring a special category means processing special category data.
claims.source: ICO guidance pages 'What is special category data?', 'Biometric recognition: key data protection concepts' and 'What about fairness, bias and discrimination?' (ico.org.uk), seen through search results, November 2026. ico.org.uk was not reachable from the build environment.

claims.claim: The Data Protection Act 2018 supplements the UK GDPR with UK-specific conditions in Schedule 1.

concept_html:
Everything a talent platform holds is personal data: names, grades, salaries, review scores, course completions, skills. It relates to an identifiable person, so the UK GDPR applies. The Data Protection Act 2018 sits beside it and adds UK-specific conditions. These lessons follow the ICO's guidance as of November 2026. Your data protection officer and legal team make the final call.

Some personal data needs more protection. The UK GDPR names nine special categories in Article 9:

  • racial or ethnic origin
  • political opinions
  • religious or philosophical beliefs
  • trade union membership
  • genetic data
  • biometric data, when you use it to identify someone uniquely
  • health
  • sex life
  • sexual orientation

Three details catch engineers out.

Biometric data is narrow. A staff photo on a profile is not special category data. The same photo used to unlock a door by face recognition is.

Inferences count. A model that infers health, ethnicity or sexual orientation from other fields processes special category data, even when no column is called that.

Protected characteristics are a different list. Age and sex are protected under the Equality Act 2010, but they are not special categories. Sexual orientation and religion are both.

To use any personal data you need a lawful basis under Article 6. To use special category data you need a lawful basis and an Article 9 condition. This is the two-part test. Lessons E1-L2 and E1-L3 cover each part.

exercises.prompt:
Write `is_special_category(field: dict) -> bool` for an attribute register. `field` has a `"category"` key, such as `"health"` or `"age"`, and may have a `"use"` key. Return True for the nine special categories. Biometric data counts only when `field.get("use") == "identify"`. Keep the category names in a module constant.

The category names are: `"racial_or_ethnic_origin"`, `"political_opinions"`, `"religious_or_philosophical_beliefs"`, `"trade_union_membership"`, `"genetic"`, `"biometric"`, `"health"`, `"sex_life"` and `"sexual_orientation"`.

The category names are: "racial_or_ethnic_origin", "political_opinions", "religious_or_philosophical_beliefs", "trade_union_membership", "genetic", "biometric", "health", "sex_life" and "sexual_orientation".
exercises.solution:
SPECIAL_CATEGORIES = frozenset(
    {
        "racial_or_ethnic_origin",
        "political_opinions",
        "religious_or_philosophical_beliefs",
        "trade_union_membership",
        "genetic",
        "biometric",
        "health",
        "sex_life",
        "sexual_orientation",
    }
)


def is_special_category(field: dict) -> bool:
    """True when an attribute is special category data under Article 9.

    Args:
        field: Register entry with a "category" and an optional "use".

    Returns:
        Whether the attribute needs an Article 9 condition.
    """
    category = field["category"]
    if category == "biometric":
        return field.get("use") == "identify"
    return category in SPECIAL_CATEGORIES

title: Personal data, special category data and the two-part test
why_html: An HR analytics team built an attrition model from absence records, overtime and the free-text reasons managers gave for sick leave. The model's strongest feature was a word count of "stress" and "anxiety" in those reasons. Nobody had flagged the column, because it was called absence_note. It held health data, so the processing needed an Article 9 condition and a data protection impact assessment that nobody had done. The model was withdrawn for three months while the team removed the field and wrote the assessment.
